title: Every path git tracks lands in one bucket with a reason

generate.repeat: Une ligne de remplissage pour dépasser le plafond du marcheur.
generate.why: Over the walker's 1 MiB default. Committing a megabyte of filler to measure a size cap would be a poor trade, so it is declared here instead of stored.

A symlink whose target is outside the repository. Generated rather than committed so the corpus stays checkout-portable, and pointed at a path that exists on every Linux and macOS. The BROKEN case is `dangling-link` beside it, and the two reasons are deliberately distinct: one resolves somewhere this tool must not read, the other resolves nowhere at all.

Declared rather than committed, because a `.gitignore` stored inside the corpus applies to THIS repository too: `secrets/token.txt` would be silently dropped from the commit and the case would fail on a fresh clone. Keeping the whole ignored-but-tracked scenario in one place is also how it stays readable.

A symlink whose target does not exist. `statSync` follows a link, so this one throws, and the walker used to drop the path in the catch before it reached any skip list. Git tracks a broken symlink like any other path — it stores the target as a blob — so the census reported it `unaccounted` and G1 failed with nothing anybody could act on. Generated rather than committed because a repository holding a dangling link is awkward to check out.

census.why: The ordinary case, present so the others are read against a baseline rather than in isolation.
Extensionless and readable. An extension-driven scanner skips it; PLAIN_TEXT_BASENAMES is why this one is not.
Same, and the file most likely to hold a sentence nobody thinks of as copy.

A `.gitignore` is where a repository writes down what it is hiding, often in prose. It has no extension of its own, so it is routed to the shell reader by NAME — it used to be `residual-sweep`, meaning nothing read it and its comments reached a person as unclassified residue rather than as a verdict.

A UTF-8 BOM is stripped before extraction, so every span in this file sits three bytes below its raw-file offset. The expectations below resolve against the decoded text for exactly that reason. Pinned byte-addressable with a claimRatio of 1, as the like-for-like control against utf16.md: the boolean is what a reader can check against the fixture, which is why it is pinned and a float would not be.

Two-byte line endings. Line and column arithmetic has to survive them without drifting. Pinned byte-addressable with a claimRatio of 1, as the like-for-like control against utf16.md: the boolean is what a reader can check against the fixture, which is why it is pinned and a float would not be.

Readable but not byte-addressable: a decoded-string offset is not a file-byte offset here, which is why `apply` refuses to patch such a file rather than writing at a plausible-looking wrong place. `claimRatio` is pinned ABSENT — `null` asserts absence — because the ratio used to divide decoded UTF-8 by raw UTF-16 and report 0.506 on a file nothing was skipped in. Dividing decoded by decoded would be worse: it mints a 1.0, and `sweep` reads a 1.0 as the extractor asserting it accounted for every byte, which is the one claim this file cannot make. Not measured is not zero.
A NUL byte makes a file binary regardless of its extension. Named as such, not lumped in with the extension-based skips.
Past the size cap. It carries text a person could read, but the cap is a deliberate refusal rather than an inability, so it is not flagged for manual verification.
The distinction the `unscannable` bucket exists for: a font carries no message, a screenshot carries the entire UI. Reporting both as 'binary' is how a translated app ships with English screenshots.
A space in the filename. Every path handed to git, to the walker and to the report has to survive it unquoted.
Tracked by git under a directory the walker refuses to descend into. Without directory-level attribution this path is simply unaccounted for and G1 fails with nothing anybody can act on.
Gitignored and tracked anyway, which happens more often than it should. The census has to attribute it rather than call it unaccounted.
Machine-generated and huge. Skipped by name, and named in the report so the skip is a decision rather than a silence.
Following it would pull bytes from outside the repository into a report that claims to describe the repository.

Named, not dropped. The reason is the entire value of this case: `unaccounted` tells a reader that this walker has a bug, and `broken-symlink` tells them their repository has a dangling link. G1 stays green because the path landed in exactly one bucket with a reason, which is the whole census claim.

Hard-wrapped prose, which is how most markdown is written. Only the LAST line of each block used to reach the inventory: the run pattern cannot cross a newline and its `$` meant end-of-block rather than end-of-line, so every line above the last failed the lookahead and was dropped — while claimRatio still reported 1.0. Measured on two real repositories, that lost roughly one prose line in five across every markdown file they had. It also carries a raw HTML block, which markdown allows anywhere: the whole line used to be skipped, so an `` — often the only description an image has — and every `` vanished from a file still reporting a claimRatio of 1.

expectations.find: Aucun d'entre eux ne doit finir sans explication.
expectations.why: Ordinary markdown prose in the source language. If this is not found, nothing else in the case means anything.

expectations.find: Construire la documentation avant de publier une version.
expectations.why: A sentence inside an extensionless build file — a place no extension-driven scanner looks.

expectations.find: Les personnes ayant contribué à ce projet
expectations.why: AUTHORS is read as prose, so the line above the names is copy while the names themselves are not.
Resolves at decoded offset 2, not raw offset 5. This expectation exists to prove the BOM was stripped without shifting every span in the file.

expectations.find: Une ligne terminée à la mode Windows.
expectations.why: The span has to land on the text and not swallow or drop the carriage return.

expectations.find: Encodé en UTF-16, comme tout ce qui sort de certains éditeurs.
expectations.why: Found and inventoried even though the file cannot be patched. A tool that skipped it would report this repository as clean while a whole file of copy sat unread.

expectations.find: La recherche accepte maintenant les accents.
expectations.why: Proves the space in the path did not stop the file being read, as opposed to merely being listed.

expectations.find: La première ligne de ce paragraphe est enveloppée à la main.
expectations.why: The first line of a multi-line paragraph. It is pinned separately from the last because the last one always worked — a fixture that only checked one line of one paragraph would have passed throughout.

expectations.find: La deuxième ligne appartient au même paragraphe et doit être trouvée.
expectations.why: A middle line, which is the case a two-line fixture cannot distinguish from an off-by-one.

expectations.find: dont la seconde ligne compte tout autant.
expectations.why: A wrapped list item. Lists take a different branch from paragraphs, so it is pinned rather than assumed to follow.

An `` inside a markdown HTML block. Half the READMEs in existence open with a `

` banner, and the alt text is frequently the only description of the image; the markdown reader hands the block to the markup extractor rather than skipping the line.

expectations.find: Ouvrir les détails de la version
expectations.why: A `<summary>`, which is a clickable label a reader sees. Pinned separately from the alt text because it is TEXT between tags rather than an attribute, and the two take different paths through the markup extractor.

pathSites.why: The filename is in the source language while the file itself is an unreadable binary. A tool treating every path as an untouchable slug reports this repository as clean; one that renames it breaks every referrer it failed to find. Refusing, and saying so, is the only correct answer.

knownGaps: A markdown HTML block is consumed only while its lines keep containing a `<`. Running to the next blank line instead was measurably worse: an HTML-ish line followed by ordinary prose swallowed the prose and handed it to a scanner that found no tags in it. The cost of the narrower rule is that a multi-line `<div>` with a blank line inside it is read as two blocks, which affects the anchor and not the recall.
